newsitem.title: GERMANY: Krupp says steel venture to be cost leader.
newsitem.headline: Krupp says steel venture to be cost leader.

text.p: Germany's Krupp group said on Friday that the merger of its steel operations with those of Thyssen AG would create a producer which would be a world-beater in terms of cost effectiveness.

Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp chief executive Gerhard Cromme told a news conference that, although his original hostile bid to take over Thyssen had failed, the deal had resolved Krupp's steel problems at a stroke.
"It will be one of the world's cost leaders," Cromme told a news conference here.

Cromme described the deal -- creating a business with output of 15 million tonnes a year and sales of 11 billion marks -- as "a fair compromise" which would allow Krupp to participate in one of the world's most profitable quality steel producers.

The price for the deal, however, is a guarantee by Krupp to ensure that Thyssen earns a minimum 300 million marks in profits from the new venture -- to be called Thyssen Krupp Stahl -- during a four-year restructuring period running to 2001.

After deducting earnings arising from the synergies created by the merger, earnings above that threshold will be split 60/40 in favour of Thyssen, in line with the venture's ownership, he told reporters.
Only when the costs of the restructuring -- including the loss of 6,600 out of 23,600 jobs through natural wastage -- are repaid, will profits be split in line with ownership.
Cromme said that restructuring costs estimated at between 800 million and 1.3 billion marks would be covered through the gains generated through synergies created by the new venture.

"Restructuring measures required to build an internationally competitive steel company after the merger of the two steel units will not be borne by Thyssen or Krupp, but by the new company," Cromme said.
"The synergies of the next few years will cover the restructuring costs. We expect that to be achieved in the next three or four years."
Krupp will, however raise the necessary short-term financing to cover those costs. Thyssen chief executive Dieter Vogel said on Thursday that his company would not bear any of the charges.
After the year 2001, gains in profitability arising from the merger will total around 550 million marks a year, Cromme said.
Despite the up-front costs, Cromme said it would still put Krupp in a better position than it would have otherwise faced.
"The results of this new company, whether good or bad, will in any event been better than those we would have achieved," he said.

Investments of around one billion marks in Krupp's Dortmund works, where operations will be scaled down from 1998, will be channelled into other new operations -- like a zinc coating plant -- to reduce the need for job losses.

Meanwhile Krupp workers, who had gone on strike during the merger talks, returned to work on Friday morning after receiving written guarantees that the merger would not bring forced job cuts -- a condition for the strike to end.
Cromme confirmed that the companies had already secured 1,700 jobs in Dortmund and had promised to create 1,300 jobs over the next four years.

The Thyssen supervisory board on Thursday gave the go-ahead to finalise the steel deal, and Cromme said he had the full backing of the Krupp board which meant that a meeting planned next week would not now be held.

Cromme said that, despite the failure of his hostile cash offer for Thyssen, banks would not have backed his bid to the tune of 15 billion marks if they had not been convinced of his strategy. Krupp was advised by Deutsche Bank AG, Dresdner Bank AG and U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs.
He also said the bid saga had opened the door slightly to the type of U.S.-style corporate takeover he said was needed to restructure German industry.
"We won't shy away again in future from following this path if -- as we are now -- we are convinced it is right," he said.
